title: Benchmarking the Pedagogical Knowledge of Large Language Models Maria Jose Ogando Portela, Jared Lee, Paul Atherton, Robin A. A. Ince, and Oliver G. B. Garrod
author: Maxime Lelievre, Amy Waldock, Meng Liu, Natalia Valdes Aspillaga, Alasdair Mackintosh,
source: arXiv preprint, AI-for-Education.org / Fab Inc (arxiv.org), July 1, 2025, 3.27.26
summary: This paper introduces The Pedagogy Benchmark, the first large-scale attempt to measure what large language models actually know about pedagogy -- teaching method and practice -- rather than just subject-matter content. Drawing on 920 multiple-choice questions from Chilean teacher-certification exams (plus a 223-question special-education/SEND supplement), the authors test 97 models spanning closed- and open-source providers, finding accuracy ranging from 28% for a small Llama model up to 89% for Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro. The authors estimate, using aggregate historical exam data, that a typical human trainee teacher would score around 50% -- meaning many current frontier models already substantially outperform the human baseline on pedagogical knowledge questions, even as costs for that level of performance have fallen sharply over 18 months. The paper charts a cost-versus-accuracy 'value frontier' to help EdTech developers pick models efficient enough for constrained deployment contexts, including offline, on-device use in low- and middle-income countries. Crucially, the authors are careful to distinguish pedagogical knowledge (what a model can state about good teaching) from pedagogical practice (whether a model can actually teach well in a live, turn-by-turn interaction), and they flag that MCQ performance says nothing about classroom management, relationship-building, or the ability to inspire and motivate learners. The paper closes by calling for ethical guardrails and human-in-the-loop safeguards as models approach or exceed human performance on this kind of knowledge test.
points: The Pedagogy Benchmark is built from genuine Chilean teacher-certification exam questions (920 general pedagogy items plus 223 SEND items), not synthetic test questions, specifically to reflect real-world pedagogical knowledge valued in actual teacher practice.

Frontier models already exceed the estimated human-teacher baseline (~50%) by a wide margin -- Gemini 2.5 Pro scores 89% -- but the authors caution that MCQ knowledge tests say nothing about classroom management or the ability to motivate real students.

At a fixed price point of $0.10 per million tokens, benchmarked accuracy rose from 50% (April 2024) to 70% (November 2024) to 82% (June 2025), illustrating how fast the cost of pedagogically competent AI has fallen in under two years.

The paper explicitly separates 'pedagogical knowledge' (what a model can state about how to teach) from 'pedagogical practice' (whether it can actually execute good teaching in a live interaction) -- a distinction relevant to anyone evaluating AI tutoring or lesson-planning tools.

The authors warn that as models approach or exceed human performance on this benchmark, the risk shifts toward over-reliance by novice teachers and the 'illusion of expertise,' making human-in-the-loop safeguards and ethical guardrails an urgent research priority.
quotes: After reviewing the LLM benchmark literature we did not find any existing LLM benchmarks which explicitly focus on knowledge of pedagogy, such as understanding of learning theories, instructional design and teaching practices.

This is a set of 920 multiple choice questions (MCQs) from teacher training exams, which evaluate LLM’s cross-domain pedagogical knowledge (CDPK). We also provide a benchmark focusing on Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND), which consists of a further 223 questions focussed on this area.

Accuracies range from 28% (Llama-3.2 1B) to 89% for the current leader, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro model. Closed-source models dominate at the top of the leaderboard (Figure 6), with 9 out of the top 10 being closed models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic.
Based on the results of more than 25,000 teachers from 2017 to 2021, the mean expected score of a human trainee teacher would be expected to be approximately 50% on The Pedagogy Benchmark.

Previous benchmarks focus on content knowledge, measuring what models know about subject matter. Evaluating pedagogical knowledge reveals what models understand about how that content can be effectively taught and assessed.

These benchmarks do not, and cannot, measure the many other critical practical dimensions of teaching, such as classroom management, student-teacher relationships, and the ability to inspire and motivate learners, all of which are fundamental to effective teaching practice.

The increasing capability of these models brings risks of misuse, such as promoting over-reliance among novice teachers, creating an illusion of expertise that could lead to harm if incorrect advice is followed, or propagating the subtle cultural and pedagogical biases inherent in their training data.
